transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-22
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Raman (CTO, LynxForge), Sam Torres (SRE), Elliot Shaw (Product Lead)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): Customer evaluating Redwood for PLG onramp with potential private needs. Interested in quickstart credits and TTFT. Wants to run benchmark and review security documentation.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intro — i'm maya, AE on the platform team at Redwood. um diego here is our solutions engineer. how are you all?
[00:10] Priya Raman: hi maya, thanks. doing well. i'm priya, cto at lynxforge. we have sam and elliot on for ops and product.
[00:18] Sam Torres: hey.
[00:20] Diego Alvarez: nice to meet you folks. quick agenda: we'll go over your goals, show how the self-serve API quickstart works (credits & TTFT), and then talk hosting fit — hosted vs dedicated vs private — and security.
[00:32] Elliot Shaw: sounds good. we have 30 minutes of context then a few Qs.

[00:40] Priya Raman: to start, high level — we're building a developer-facing assistant for our platform to help customers with infra troubleshooting. most requests will be diagnostic and will include partial customer identifiers (hashed ids, not plaintext), so PII is a concern. initial plan is PLG — let devs try features via our app, measure engagement, then scale.
[01:05] Maya Chen: got it. so primary concerns: data residency, PII, cost, and latency? anything else for success criteria?
[01:12] Priya Raman: yep. also time-to-first-token — we want devs to get quick responses in the web IDE. target p95 generation latency is under 300ms for short prompts (<= 128 tokens).
[01:26] Diego Alvarez: that's helpful. our hosted API can easily hit sub-300ms for smaller models in many regions; dedicated gives more predictable tail-latency, and private (VPC or on-prem) is for when you need strict network isolation or specific KMS/HSM keys.

[02:00] Sam Torres: quick question — with hosted, how does data retention work? we can't have raw logs stored indefinitely.
[02:08] Maya Chen: standard hosted flow: request payloads are ephemeral by default, we have configurable retention policies and can opt-out of logging at request level. we also support customer-managed encryption keys in dedicated/private setups. note: i'll send the SOC2 + security pack after the call.
[02:28] Elliot Shaw: ok. and free credits — how do we get started?
[02:33] Maya Chen: we give onboarding credits for PLG experimentation plus a quickstart repo. typical TTFT path: 1) grab quickstart creds, 2) run sample prompt set locally or in staging, 3) measure token costs and latency. with our SDK it's usually minutes to first request for engineers.
[02:55] Priya Raman: minutes sounds good. do you have examples of real runs and how you measure time-to-first-token?
[03:04] Diego Alvarez: yes — we provide scripts that warm the KV cache and emulate bursty traffic; TTFT commonly means the time from issuing first API call to receiving first token stream — warming strategies and small prefetch caches help. we'll share a repo with benchmark scripts.

[03:40] Speaker 1: (mumbled) and what's the typical cost per inference for these diagnostic prompts?
[03:45] Maya Chen: depends on model and sequence length; for a 128 token gen on a 7B quantized model you're usually in the low single-digit cents per call. for high throughput we recommend batching and caching.
[03:58] Priya Raman: right, and do you have guidance on model selection? we want accuracy vs cost tradeoff — not necessarily the largest model.
[04:07] Diego Alvarez: absolutely. our Optimize tool suggests model + quantization profiles by workload. for diagnostics, many customers pick a 7B or 13B quantized variant and tune prompt/temperature; we can run comparisons during the pilot.

[04:30] Elliot Shaw: can you explain the Dedicated offering briefly? was that reserved GPU pools?
[04:36] Maya Chen: yes — Dedicated is reserved capacity, predictable throughput, and tenancy isolation. it comes with autoscaling policies and optional burst for traffic spikes. we can attach VPC peering for network controls.
[04:50] Sam Torres: if we start with hosted and then move to dedicated, how disruptive is that?
[04:55] Diego Alvarez: we design the API to be identical across modes. requests, SDKs, and rollout policies are the same — mainly a config change and potential model pinning. data plane network configs differ for private. migration is usually straightforward.

[05:20] Priya Raman: we also have to show security to our compliance board — SOC2 type II, SSO, RBAC, audit logs, KMS integration. can you cover which of those are supported out-of-the-box?
[05:33] Maya Chen: yes. SOC2 reports available, SSO via SAML/OIDC for console, RBAC on API keys and tokens, audit trails for token usage and admin actions. KMS integrations are available for dedicated & private; for hosted we offer BYOK via envelope encryption in supported regions.
[05:53] Priya Raman: cool. what about egress to our VPC for private deployments? do you support VPC endpoints or direct connect?
[06:02] Diego Alvarez: for Private we support VPC peering and private endpoints. on-prem air-gapped options exist for regulated customers but that's a heavier lift.

[06:20] Elliot Shaw: i'm curious about telemetry — do we get token-level cost breakdowns? we need that to instrument our billing buckets.
[06:27] Maya Chen: yes, the Console exposes token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route and model. you can export CSVs or hook to our billing API.

[06:40] Sam Torres: what's the usual timeline to run a small pilot and get meaningful metrics? two weeks?
[06:46] Diego Alvarez: two weeks is a solid target: week 0 onboarding + quickstart, week 1 run benchmark & tune, week 2 analyze results and decide on scale or dedicated trial. if you want reserved capacity we can parallelize procurement.

[07:05] Priya Raman: procurement is usually slow for us, but initial pilot shouldn't require legal for a credits trial, right?
[07:12] Maya Chen: correct, credits + self-serve quickstart are self-serve. dedicated/reserved capacity requires an order and SOW.

[07:25] Elliot Shaw: any gotchas with SDKs? our stack is Node + a Go microservice for async work.
[07:31] Diego Alvarez: we have language SDKs for Node, Go, Python. async patterns are covered; we also have sample serverless integrations. the quickstart repo includes Node and Go examples.

[07:50] Speaker 2: (brief aside) do you support tool calling / function calling?
[07:54] Diego Alvarez: yes — streaming + function calling are supported; you can structure outputs or call endpoints.

[08:10] Priya Raman: one more question — PII: even if we hash identifiers, there's still risk. would we need private for initial pilot?
[08:18] Maya Chen: hashing helps but is not a silver bullet. many teams start hosted with request-level logging disabled and strict retention; if your compliance board requires no third-party egress of any sensitive tokens, then Private is safest. we can scope a hybrid: keep dev traffic on hosted credits and route production PII-bearing requests to Private.

[08:45] Elliot Shaw: that hybrid approach might map to our rollout — dev & PLG flows on hosted credits, production on dedicated or private.

[09:00] Maya Chen: for the free credits onboarding, the path is: we provision trial credits to your org, you use quickstart code, run benchmark scripts (we provide sample prompts), and share results. we can attach a short 1-week reserved window if you need predictable perf for demo days.

[09:25] Priya Raman: ok, let's talk numbers — what does a minimal pilot look like? say 10k calls per day for a week — any expectations on cost / compute?
[09:34] Diego Alvarez: rough math: if average call is 100 tokens generation, at 0.01 per 1k tokens (example), that equates to about X — sorry, transcription: numbers varies — we'll send a modeled cost sheet. this is why we recommend running the benchmark; caching and batching can drop unit cost significantly.

[10:05] Sam Torres: can you also show us a sample of dispatch rules? we want fallback in case of latency spike or capacity issues.
[10:12] Maya Chen: yes — our routing can fall back to a cheaper model or different region; there are automated policies for A/B and canary rollouts. we'll include a routing examples doc in the materials.

[10:35] Elliot Shaw: hypothetically, if we auto-scale to 1k QPS, is that supported with dedicated?
[10:41] Diego Alvarez: dedicated can be configured for high throughput, but 1k QPS depends on model size, batching, and concurrency. we usually benchmark that during scoping.

[11:00] Priya Raman: from a technical checklist perspective for us to greenlight pilot: 1) time-to-first-token < 300ms on p95 for short prompts, 2) documentation and quickstart working in our staging, 3) security pack reviewed.
[11:15] Maya Chen: noted — we'll prioritize tests for p95 latency and a focused quickstart.

[11:28] Speaker 3: (crosstalk) do you support EU data residency?
[11:31] Maya Chen: yes — we have regions and can enforce residency via routing; for strict residency Private is easiest.

[11:45] Diego Alvarez: i'll add that our quickstart includes terraform snippets for VPC peering and sample KMS integration steps.

[12:00] Elliot Shaw: sounds great. any limitations on model fine-tuning or adapters?
[12:07] Maya Chen: hosted supports fine-tuning ops via our managed workflows for certain models, but for private/on-prem you may bring your own fine-tune pipelines. fine-tuning availability varies by model license.

[12:25] Priya Raman: ok, let's talk operational cadence — after pilot who would we engage for a deeper performance scoping?
[12:32] Maya Chen: our SE team (diego and I) + a performance engineer join a 60–90 minute technical deep dive to run specific benchmarks and map capacity. we'll propose dates after you sign off on the pilot scope.

[12:50] Elliot Shaw: can you include an example SLO we can show our stakeholders?
[12:55] Diego Alvarez: yes; we'll include a sample SLO doc — p95 < 300ms, availability 99.9% for dedicated, etc.

[13:10] Priya Raman: any legal prerequisites even for the credit trial? NDA or DPA?
[13:15] Maya Chen: usually a DPA is standard for production egress; for trials we can execute a limited DPA. legal can be cc'd later — i'll surface contact.

[13:30] Sam Torres: what about observability integrations — e.g., can we stream trace data to our datadog?
[13:36] Diego Alvarez: yes, we have hooks for traces and metrics; you can forward logs or export metrics into Datadog/Prometheus.

[13:50] Elliot Shaw: ok last question from me — what's the best way to demo quick wins to internal stakeholders?
[13:55] Maya Chen: show a short video or live demo of TTFT and a sample user flow in your app, plus numbers from the quickstart benchmark comparing model choices. the credits let you set up a demo environment quickly.

[14:12] Priya Raman: that's helpful. how will we measure success of the pilot?
[14:17] Maya Chen: define clear metrics: latency SLO adherence, cost per action threshold, and developer engagement (DAU for the new feature). if pilot meets thresholds we can discuss reserved capacity.

[14:35] Diego Alvarez: i'll put together the quickstart repo link, sample prompt set, and benchmark scripts after the call — and include CLI commands to measure TTFT and token-level cost.

[14:50] Maya Chen: sounds like we have good alignment. any blockers?
[14:54] Priya Raman: internal procurement timeline may be a blocker for reserved capacity but not for credits. we'll confirm stakeholders and compliance constraints by 10/28 as discussed.

[15:10] Maya Chen: great — recap: i'll send hosting comparison + security pack and pricing sheet; diego will send quickstart + benchmark scripts; priya will confirm pilot stakeholders and constraints. then we schedule the pilot kickoff.
[15:30] Elliot Shaw: thanks all. looking forward to the repo.
[15:33] Sam Torres: thanks.
[15:35] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. bye.

(Transcript ends — occasional filler and automatic speaker labeling errors present.)
